items.cite: Finn Benestad and Dag Schjelderup-Ebbe, *Edvard Grieg: The Man and the Artist*, translated by William H. Halverson and Leland B. Sateren (University of Nebraska Press, 1988).
items.note: The standard life and works of a Bergen merchant’s son, with letters, diaries and music examples in a parallel column.

items.cite: Daniel M. Grimley, *Grieg: Music, Landscape and Norwegian Identity* (Boydell Press, 2006).
items.note: On what “Norwegian” meant in Grieg’s music and who decided it. Reads the Lyric Pieces, Peer Gynt and the folk-tune settings against the landscape and politics of the time.

items.cite: Finn Benestad, “Edvard Grieg”, *Norsk biografisk leksikon* (Store norske leksikon).
items.note: A dense, dated account in Norwegian by the editor of Grieg’s letters of where and when each work and each meeting happened, with quotations from the letters and diaries.
The American critic quotes Grieg’s own words on Liszt, Nordraak and his songs, from Grieg’s letters to him and from his letter to his parents about Liszt playing the concerto at sight.

items.cite: Finn Benestad and William H. Halverson, eds., *Edvard Grieg: Diaries, Articles, Speeches* (Peer Gynt Press, 2001).
items.note: Grieg’s diaries, articles and speeches in English, on music, politics and his own life. Edited by Finn Benestad, who also edited his letters.

items.cite: Edvard Grieg Archive, Bergen Public Library.
items.note: In 1906 Grieg and Nina left his manuscripts, letters and printed music to Bergen Public Library, which keeps the Grieg archive and has put his letters to Tchaikovsky online.
